🌍 AI in your world · Lesson 13 · 2 min read

Data: The Fuel of AI

Where the examples that AI learns from come from, how they go wrong, and why a model is always tested on examples it has never seen.

Where data comes from

A model learns only from its examples, its dataset. Some data is collected on purpose: photos, recordings, survey answers. Much more is left behind as we use apps: every search, click, like and pause. Sensors add more: phones, watches, cars and weather stations measure things all day. For many tasks, each example also needs a label, the right answer (“cat”, “spam”, “healthy leaf”). Labels are often added by people, one example at a time.

Did you know? Behind many famous AI systems are thousands of people who labelled data by hand: drawing boxes around cars, marking which answers are helpful, or sorting photos. This work is real, and it is often low-paid.

Garbage in, garbage out

Real data is messy. Some values are missing, some are typed wrong (“dgo” instead of “dog”), some examples appear twice, and some are impossible (a 150-year-old student). A model can't tell a mistake from a fact: it learns from both. So data scientists spend much of their time cleaning: finding and fixing problems before training. A model can also learn a shortcut that happens to be in the data instead of the real thing.

Did you know? Researchers found that a model for spotting skin cancer in photos had partly learned that a ruler in the picture means “worrying”, because doctors often measure spots they are worried about. The model looked clever, but it had learned the ruler, not the skin.

Train and test

How do you know a model is good? Not by asking it about the examples it learned from: it may simply have memorised them. So before training, we put some examples aside: the test set. The model never learns from them. Its score on the test set is a fair guess of how it will do on new, real examples. A model that is great on training data and much worse on the test set has overfitted: it learned the details, not the rule.

Whose data?

Data is about people, so it comes with questions. Did people agree to their data being used? Could it reveal something private? Does it include everyone the model will be used on? A face dataset made mostly of one group of people will work worse for others: the model's bias starts in the data. Good datasets are documented: where the data came from, who is in it, what is missing.

Did you know? Laws like the EU's GDPR give people rights over their data, such as the right to see what a company keeps about them and to ask for it to be deleted.

Key points

  • A model learns only from its examples; many examples need a label, often added by people.
  • Messy data (missing, wrong, repeated or impossible values) teaches a model mistakes, so data is cleaned first.
  • A model is judged on a test set it never learned from; great on training but worse on tests means overfitting.

Check yourself

You train a model on 1,000 photos and then test it on the same 1,000 photos. It scores 100%. What does that tell you?

Show the answer

Right answer: Very little: it may have memorised them, so you need to test it on new photos

A model can memorise its training examples, so a score on them says little. Only a test on examples it has never seen shows whether it learned the rule. The photos weren't necessarily easy: the test just wasn't fair.
